This message comes from Angie. Angie has been helping homeowners find skilled pros
to get their home projects done well for over 30 years. For everything from minor repairs
to major remodels, find reviews, pricing, and booking at Angie.com or on the Angie app.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman. The president of Cornell University responded
Saturday to charges by a student that she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024.
New York's governor said Friday the investigation into the charges was flawed. President Michael
Kotlikoff released a video statement saying the university must do better. "There are real legal
and privacy limits on what we can say, but we will make a greater effort to explain what we can,
to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken, and to be more transparent."
The New York State Attorney General is now taking over that investigation.
President Trump says he won't ban U.S. diesel exports to Europe after G7 countries announced
Friday they would release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from national reserves.
As Terry Schultz reports, Trump pressured the European members of the group to make the move
to help ease fuel prices in the U.S. ahead of midterm elections.
The G7, which includes the four biggest European economies plus the European Union,
agreed to tap emergency inventories after President Trump demanded they help curb the
rise of fuel prices caused primarily by the U.S. war on Iran. European leaders had been reluctant
to contribute from their fuel stocks. Analyst Maximilian Terhale of Cambridge University's
Center for Geopolitics says they should have used the situation to remind the often critical Trump
that he needs them as allies. "It's somewhat desperate and we need to, in a friendly way,
manipulate that desperation." It's not clear how much of the fuel will come from each country's
reserves to make up the announced 100 million barrels. For NPR News, I'm Terry Schultz in Brussels.
Multiple data centers are being planned for Louisiana. Many communities there have been
resistant to those data centers, in part because of their use of power and water resources.
Arbor Juhas of the Gold State Newsroom reports that community colleges are preparing local
residents for new jobs there. At Louisiana Delta Community College in Monroe, about a
dozen students are learning to build and maintain data centers. I'm going to pass around some safety
glasses. Local businesses often rely on community colleges to provide the training people need to
work for them. In Northeast Louisiana, the biggest business right now is meta. The tech giant is
building its largest data center here and it needs thousands of workers. Since January, more than a
hundred people have graduated from Delta's new programs, which they launched with meta support.
The college says all of the graduates are working. Some thought they'd have to leave the area to find
work and say they're glad to have an option closer to home. For NPR News, I'm Opera Juhas. The
Commissioner of Tennessee's Department of Corrections is resigning after a botched execution attempt on
Wednesday. Frank Strada says his departure is in the best interests of the state. You're listening to
NPR News. Voters in Brazil will take to the polls on Sunday to elect a new president. Current
President Luis Inacio Lula da Silva held a pre-election parade Saturday in downtown Sao Paulo,
while opposition candidate Flavio Bolsonaro visited several cities in Brazil's countryside,
Sao Paulo State as the country's major center where 20 percent of the nation's vote is based.
The Trump administration is giving the public more time to comment on its proposal for unprecedented
changes to the next U.S. census. The plan would reshape the drawing of voting maps and the
distribution of federal funding across the country, and Perez-Hansi Luong reports.
Public comments will now be accepted through November 2nd. The proposal calls for excluding
millions of U.S. residents from a census tally that, according to the 14th Amendment,
must include the "whole number of persons" in each state. That count is used to determine
each state's share of congressional seats and electoral college votes for a decade.
The Trump administration argues the Constitution's framers did not intend for the word "persons"
to include people living in the states without U.S. citizenship or a green card. Trump officials
also propose cutting questions about race and ethnicity because they see a "reduced need"
for that information, which is used for civil rights enforcement. If the proposal is finalized,
it's expected to spark lawsuits, and Congress or a new presidential administration in 2029 could
reverse any census changes that Trump officials make. Hansi Luong, NPR News.
President Trump Saturday posted online the personal cell phone number of Arkansas Republican
Senator Tom Cotton hears people to call Cotton to demand that he help pass a measure to make
daylight saving time permanent. The bill passed the House in July. Trump argues that the bill
would provide more daylight during the times Americans are "most active." I'm Dale Willman,
NPR News. This message comes from Jerry. Noticing your car insurance rate creep up
